headline: Global Connectivity for Digital Nomads: A Complete Guide
description: How to stay online in any country: eSIMs, VPNs, banking-safe connections, the travel hardware to carry and what to do when the network fails.
keywords: eSIM, VPN, Digital nomads, Travel hardware, Travel Wi-Fi
articleBody:
A woman working at a laptop on a sunny terrace

Global Connectivity for Digital Nomads

Reliable internet is the one tool a remote worker cannot do without. This guide covers the layers of a connection that does not fail, the eSIM and VPN choices that go with it, how to keep your bank and your verification codes working, and the travel hardware worth carrying.

Key takeaways. Build three layers: mobile data, a second route and an emergency option. Install a travel eSIM before you fly, and keep your home number as a second line. Use a VPN for public Wi-Fi, blocked websites and banking. Carry a charger, a travel plug adapter and an extension cord. Keep your power bank in your hand luggage.

Build three layers of connection

Nobody can promise that the network never fails, but you can make sure that one failure never stops your work. Think in three layers. Mobile data is your main connection: a travel eSIM or a local SIM, shared with your laptop as a hotspot. Wi-Fi is your second route: your accommodation, a coworking space or a café. An emergency option is for the day both fail: a second SIM on another network, an old phone with a second SIM or eSIM that you keep charged and use as a hotspot, or a place you can walk to that has a reliable connection. Each layer should work without the others. Test the one you plan to use before an important call, and know which one you would switch to. That habit prevents most dropped calls and missed deadlines.

eSIM or physical SIM

An eSIM is a SIM built into the phone. You install it with a QR code or a link, so you can buy a plan before you fly and have data the moment you land. A physical SIM is the card in the tray. Most recent phones take an eSIM, but an iPhone has to be an XS or later , and a phone locked to its carrier may refuse a plan from another provider. Check before you buy, not at the airport.

eSIM or physical SIM How you get it: Online, before you fly, At a shop or kiosk in the country. Changing plans: Install another plan on the phone, Swap the card. Works with: Phones that support eSIM and are not locked to a carrier, Almost any phone with a SIM tray. Keeping your home number: Yes, on a dual-SIM phone: the home SIM stays in the tray, Only with a second SIM slot, or by swapping cards

For a trip of a few weeks or more, an eSIM is the better choice: you set it up before you fly and you keep your home SIM. A physical SIM is the option when your phone does not support an eSIM. A local SIM card can be worth it for a long stay in one country, because you get a local number, and in some countries you can get a local SIM as an eSIM as well. Know the price: almost everywhere you have to register your personal details and show your passport, so the phone company of every country where you buy one holds your details. That is a privacy concern.

Which kind of plan

Travel plans come in three forms. Which one suits you depends on how much you work on mobile data and how predictable the speed must be.

Three kinds of mobile data plan How it works: A fixed number of gigabytes for a number of days, A price per day, with data described as unlimited, Prepaid at a shop in the country, topped up there. Watch out for: Running out during a busy week; check that you can top up, A fair-use policy that can reduce your speed, Registering your personal details and passport, almost everywhere, and a local number. Suits: Light users and short trips, Heavy users who accept some limits, Long stays in one country

To compare what plans cost, here are two for 30 days in Thailand.

Plans for 30 days in Thailand Prices in US dollars Nomad: $8, $10. Saily eSIM: $7.99, $10.99. Airalo: $8, $11. Ubigi: Not available, $11 Prices change, so look at the provider before you buy. Ubigi does not sell a plan smaller than 10 GB for 30 days.

The prices are within a dollar of each other, so price should not decide. Look at the countries you will visit, how easy a top-up is and how you pay.

Airalo (opens in a new tab) sells both plans with a set amount of data and unlimited plans priced by the day, and it has a global eSIM. It is the one to look at if you want to choose between the two kinds at one provider, or if you cross many borders.

Nomad (opens in a new tab) offers plans in many sizes, from a short stay with a little data to a short stay with a lot. Choose it if you want to match the amount of data closely to your trip.

Saily eSIM (opens in a new tab) comes from Nord Security, the company behind NordVPN. It suits you if you want your eSIM and your VPN from one company.

Ubigi (opens in a new tab) sells prepaid plans for single countries, regions and the world, without extra fees. Choose it if you want one plan for a region instead of a plan per country.

Holafly (opens in a new tab) sells only unlimited data, priced by the day, and has a global plan as well. It suits people who do not want to count gigabytes and accept the fair-use rules described below. The table beside this paragraph shows its prices in Thailand, as an example.

Holafly, unlimited data. In Thailand, in US dollars. 3 days: $11.90. 5 days: $20.50. 7 days: $27.50. 10 days: $36.50. 15 days: $50.50. 30 days: $73.90

Your bank may sell one too

Some fintech banks sell a travel eSIM in their app, which lets you pay from the account you already use.

Revolut (opens in a new tab) sells prepaid eSIM data plans under Lifestyle in its app, for single countries, regions or the world. You need an eSIM phone that is not carrier-locked, and your home number stays on the physical SIM.

Wise (opens in a new tab) sells eSIM plans from the Travel hub of its app, for about 150 countries. Its global plans are valid for 12 months from the first connection, so keep the eSIM off until you land.

The advantage of a bank is paying from the account you already use, not a lower price. Compare its plan with the providers above, and with a travel eSIM bought directly.

Compare the plans

Not all providers list their plans and prices on their public website, and in the app you may have to sign up before you see them. The buttons below let you compare the plans of two major providers.

See Airalo's global plans

See Holafly's global plans

Why unlimited slows down

“Unlimited” on a travel eSIM rarely means the same speed all month. The network operator in the country applies a fair-usage policy, and the provider has to follow it. Holafly’s Thailand page, for example, says speed can be reduced in rare cases, for no more than a day, and does not say at what amount of data it starts. To avoid surprises: Read the plan description for “fair use”, “daily”, “throttled” or “reduced speed” before you pay. Look for a daily limit, not only the headline. Check that sharing data with your laptop (hotspot or tethering) is allowed. Some plans limit it. If you rely on video calls, a fixed amount of data is the safer choice: the speed you pay for is the speed you get until the data is gone.

Keep your bank and payment accounts working

Banks watch for unusual logins. A new country, a public network and a VPN address that changes every day all look unusual, and an account can be locked at the worst moment. Tell your bank or card issuer that you are travelling , if its app has a way to do that. Log in once from a stable connection soon after you arrive, not for the first time from an airport network. Keep your exit address the same. If you use a VPN, pick one server in the same country each time, or use a dedicated IP address that only you use. Prefer an authenticator app or a security key over text-message codes. A dedicated IP address reduces the repeated checks that a changing address causes, but it does not guarantee that a bank will accept you.

Keep receiving verification codes

Many banks and apps still send login codes by text message to the number on file. If you swap your home SIM for a travel SIM, those messages go nowhere.

The fix is a dual-SIM phone. Many recent phones, iPhone and Android, can keep two numbers active at once, a physical SIM plus an eSIM. On an iPhone, for example, only one number at a time uses cellular data . Keep your home SIM in the tray, set the travel eSIM as your data line, and turn off data roaming on the home line so it does not use data abroad.

Texts to your home number can still arrive, if your home carrier allows roaming for messages. Ask your carrier what that costs before you leave. If you have trouble receiving text messages, it can help to turn off automatic network selection on the home SIM and choose a carrier manually. Move your important accounts to an authenticator app as well, so a login does not depend on a phone number.

Dual SIM settings on an Android phone: home SIM for calls and texts, travel eSIM for mobile data

Do you need a VPN, and which kind?

A VPN encrypts the traffic between your device and the VPN server, so whoever runs a public network cannot read it. It also hides your real address from the sites you visit. It does not make you anonymous, and it does not make your connection faster. Nomads use one for four reasons: safer public Wi-Fi; reaching websites that the government of the country you stay in blocks; using content from your home country that is geo-blocked abroad; a stable address for banking.

Three ways to run a VPN What it is: A subscription with many servers, shared by many users, The same subscription plus an address that only you use, A server you run at home or on a rented machine. Best for: Public Wi-Fi, blocked websites and geo-blocked content, Banking and sites that block shared addresses, Reaching your own devices, with a stable address. Effort: Install an app, Install an app and buy an add-on, Set it up and keep it updated yourself

NordVPN (opens in a new tab) sells a dedicated IP as an add-on: an address reserved for you, usable on up to 10 devices at once with OpenVPN and on one with NordLynx . It costs the same on every plan and, on a one-year plan, $5.89 a month.

ExpressVPN (opens in a new tab) lets you connect up to 14 devices at once on its highest tier. A dedicated IP comes with that tier and is a separate purchase on the others. If a dedicated IP will not connect, ExpressVPN advises switching the protocol to Lightway.

Surfshark (opens in a new tab) allows unlimited simultaneous connections. Its dedicated IP is a separate add-on from $3.75 a month, in 20 locations, and you cannot change the location after you get it.

Proton VPN (opens in a new tab) has a free plan with no data limit, but it allows one connection at a time. Mullvad (opens in a new tab) costs 5 euros a month at any length of subscription (its page shows $5.60), works on up to five devices and takes anonymous payment, including cash by post.

If you prefer to run your own, WireGuard is a modern VPN protocol designed to be easy to configure. Tailscale (opens in a new tab) builds on it to connect your own devices, and its personal plan is free for up to six users with unlimited devices.

For public Wi-Fi, blocked websites and geo-blocked content, any of the commercial VPNs does the job. For banking, a dedicated IP is the extra to look at, and you pay for it. Run your own server only if you like to tinker.

NordVPN and Saily eSIM (opens in a new tab) are both from Nord Security, so you might find a special deal when you buy a VPN and an eSIM from the same company.

See NordVPN's offers

Wi-Fi in the places you stay

Most nomads stay in homestays, rentals and coworking spaces, where the Wi-Fi is the host’s: you cannot change its speed or its router. On the first day, run a speed test and a video call before you rely on it for work, and keep mobile data as your second layer.

Login pages in hotels, airports and trains

Many public networks show a login page where you accept terms or enter a room number, and many places allow only a few devices per room. At airports, and maybe on trains, you cannot always log in on your laptop either. A phone connected to such a network may or may not be able to share it with your laptop as a hotspot (Wi-Fi sharing or internet sharing).

GL.iNet Beryl AX. GL-MT3000. Wi-Fi: Wi-Fi 6. Ports: 2.5G WAN port, 1G LAN port. VPN: WireGuard and OpenVPN built in, as client or server. WireGuard speed: Up to 300 Mbps. Weight: 196 g (6.9 oz). Price: $98.99

A travel router solves the device limit: you connect it to the network once, log in on the router, and it makes its own Wi-Fi network that all your devices join as one device. The GL.iNet Beryl AX (GL-MT3000) (opens in a new tab) is a pocket-sized Wi-Fi 6 router with WireGuard and OpenVPN built in, and it can act as a VPN client or a VPN server. It costs $98.99, also on Amazon (opens in a new tab) .

A travel router is worth it if you often stay in places with a login page or a device limit.

GL.iNet Beryl AX travel router Photo: User_Pascal (opens in a new tab)

What hardware to carry

A few small things keep your devices charged and your connection running wherever you stay. This is the kit to pack, with a closer look at one charger and one travel plug adapter.

The kit. A multi-port GaN charger. A travel plug adapter. An extension cord. A power bank, in your hand luggage. A travel router. A backup SIM or an old phone

Anker Charger 100W with 3 Ports and Smart Display Photo: Anker (opens in a new tab)

We recommend looking into the Anker Charger 100W with 3 Ports and Smart Display (opens in a new tab) . It has two USB-C ports and one USB-A port, 100 W in total, and Anker lists the MacBook Air and Pro as compatible. It costs $69.99.

Plug types differ per country, so a travel plug adapter is what makes your charger fit the wall socket. Anker makes a very small and light one, which weighs next to nothing in a bag.

Anker Nano Travel Adapter

Bring a plain extension cord of about 10 feet (3 meters), not a power strip, which takes space and is heavy. A wall socket is often not where you want it, and a travel adapter with a heavy MacBook charger makes the plug fall out of the socket. On an extension cord, the charger can lie on a table or the floor.

Keep your power bank in your hand luggage: spare lithium batteries and power banks may not travel in checked bags, and batteries of 101 to 160 Wh need approval from the airline . Read the watt-hours on its label, not the milliamp-hours.

When the connection fails

Work through these steps in order. Most problems are solved in the first three. Check the basics: airplane mode is off, mobile data is on, and the travel eSIM is the line selected for data. Check data roaming. Most travel eSIMs need it switched on for the travel line. Restart the phone, then choose the network manually and try another one from the list. Open your provider’s app or help page and check whether the plan is active and has data left. Switch to your second layer: Wi-Fi, a hotspot from another phone, or your backup SIM. If nothing works, move to a place with a reliable connection, such as a coworking space, and tell your client that you will be back online shortly.

Pre-trip checklist. Check that your phone supports eSIM and is not locked to a carrier.. Buy and install your travel eSIM while you still have a connection, and switch it on when you land.. Keep your home SIM active as a second line, and turn off data roaming on it.. Move important accounts from text-message codes to an authenticator app.. Tell your bank you are travelling, if its app lets you.. Install your VPN app and sign in before you leave.. Pack your charger, travel plug adapter and extension cord.. Charge your power bank and pack it in your hand luggage.. Download offline maps and your booking details.. Save your provider’s support contact where you can read it offline.

Still have questions?

Quick answers to common questions about staying connected while you travel and work.

Can I use my home carrier abroad instead? You can, but roaming charges and limits vary a lot between carriers and plans. Check your plan’s roaming terms before you leave, and compare them with a travel eSIM for the countries you will visit. Is hotel Wi-Fi safe for banking? Use your mobile data or a VPN for banking when you can. If you have to use the hotel network, make sure the app or site uses HTTPS and keep your devices updated. Can I share my phone’s data with my laptop? Yes, on most phones this is the hotspot or tethering setting. Check that your plan allows it, because some plans limit or block it. How much data do I need? It depends on how you work. Email and chat use little, and video calls use much more. Count your call hours, then pick a plan with room to spare or one that you can top up. Does a VPN slow my connection down? Usually a little, because your traffic takes a detour through the VPN server. A server close to you keeps the difference small.

Most people only think about mobile data when it has already stopped working: the plane lands, the phone finds a network it does not recognise, and a message appears about roaming charges. A little planning before the trip turns that moment into a non-event. This guide walks through the choices in the order you will actually meet them, from the phone in your pocket to the first morning in a new country. Text The first thing to find out is whether your phone can use an eSIM at all. Most phones sold in the last four years can, but carrier-locked models often cannot take a second plan until the lock is removed. Open the settings, look for a line called the EID or a mention of a digital SIM, and write down what you find while you still have a connection. The second thing is the lock itself. A phone bought on a monthly plan is frequently tied to the carrier that sold it, and unlocking can take a few days. Request it early, because a request made at the airport will not be answered before you board. Unlocked, locked and in between A fully unlocked phone accepts any SIM or eSIM from any provider, which is what you want. A locked phone only accepts the carrier that sold it, and some carriers unlock automatically once the device is paid off. If you are unsure, the quickest test is to put in a SIM from another network and see whether it is recognised. Phones bought abroad add a further wrinkle, because the radio bands can differ between regions. A model sold in North America may miss a band that is common in Europe or Asia, so coverage can be thinner than the map suggests. The manufacturer's specification page lists the bands, and a provider's coverage page lists the ones it uses. What the settings screen tells you On most phones the relevant information sits under a menu named for the network, the SIM or the general device information. Look for a line saying the phone is unlocked or that there are no restrictions on the SIM. If the wording is vague, a screenshot of the screen is enough for a provider's support team to answer. It also helps to note the model number and the software version while you are there. Providers occasionally ask for both, and the answer decides whether a plan can be installed at all. Keep the screenshot in a place you can open without a connection. Small details that save a support call Write the order number and the email address you used on a card or a note that is not stored on the phone. If the phone is the thing that fails, you will want that information somewhere else. A paper copy in the passport sleeve costs nothing and has rescued many a first evening. Do the same for the plan's activation details, such as the code or the address you were sent. Some providers send them once and never again, so a lost message can mean a new purchase. Take a photo of the screen as soon as it appears. One last thing before you leave the house Turn off automatic updates for apps while you are on a metered plan, and download the maps and the tickets you will need for the first day. The phone will then behave itself on its first hour abroad, and you can spend that hour looking around instead of watching a progress bar. Its corners are round, since it stops short of the screen edges. In the wide column The variant wide: 4/3 on a phone, then 16/7. In the reading column No variant: 4/3 on a phone, then 16/9. The same band can carry a looping silent clip instead of a still. It is always autoplay, muted and controls-less (that is what makes it a background rather than a video you play), and under prefers-reduced-motion the clip is hidden and its poster paints in its place, with no JavaScript involved. A looping background clip A band with a moving background A looping, silent clip, still under reduced motion. Layouts A page is a stack of layouts . Each layout is a web component with its own markup and its own CSS (its slots, its widths, its gaps and where it changes), and the components in each of its slots stack. What works. Installed before you fly, working the moment you land, with no queue and no kiosk.. No passport photocopy at a kiosk.. Keeps your home number live for two-factor codes. What doesn't. Usually dearer per gigabyte than a local SIM.. Data only, with no local number for taxis or deliveries.. Older phones cannot use it at all. Long text in one column and an image in the other. name: About Movelli: independent guides for people on the move
description: Movelli publishes plain, fast-loading guides to eSIMs, VPNs, travel gear and money for people who live and work abroad. Here is who we are and how the site earns.
articleBody:
About Movelli

Movelli is an independent publication of practical guides to staying connected and managing money while you live and work across borders. Here is what we publish, who stands behind it, and how the site pays for itself.

What is Movelli? Movelli is an independent publisher of practical guides for people who live, work and travel across borders. We write about the things a long stay depends on: mobile data and eSIMs, VPNs, travel routers, chargers and everyday money abroad. Every guide is written for someone who moves between homestays, rentals and coworking spaces, not for a one-off holiday. The pages are light and quick to load, so they still work on a weak connection in a new country.

Working remotely, wherever the stay is Photo: Aleh Tsikhanau (opens in a new tab)

Who is behind Movelli? Movelli is written by people who live and work on the move themselves, and the guides come from that daily use: what works on arrival, what breaks, and what is worth paying for. If a guide gets something wrong, or a price or rule has changed, tell us with the form below and we will correct it. How does Movelli make money? Some links in our guides are affiliate links. If you buy a product or a plan through one, Movelli may earn a commission, and the price you pay stays the same. Any page that carries such links says so in a note under its introduction. Prices change, so wherever a guide shows one it names the exact plan and says that it can move. Our global connectivity guide is a good place to see how a guide is built.

Get in touch Send message

Prefer to follow along? Subscribe to our RSS feed for new and updated guides. © 2026 Movelli.

Privacy Policy

Movelli is built to respect your privacy by default. We don’t run analytics, we don’t set tracking cookies, and we don’t ask you to log in or hand over personal data to read anything. What we collect Almost nothing. There are no accounts and no advertising trackers on this site. If you write to us through the contact form , we receive the name, email and message you submit — used only to reply to your enquiry, never for marketing. Like any website, our host keeps standard server logs (such as IP address and requested page) for security and to understand aggregate traffic. These are not used to build a profile of you. Cookies and local storage We don’t set cookies. If you install Movelli as an app or browse it normally, your browser’s Service Worker stores copies of pages and assets on your device so the site loads fast and works offline. That cache never leaves your device and you can clear it any time from your browser settings. Links to other sites When you follow an outbound link to a provider (see our affiliate disclosure ), you’re subject to that company’s privacy policy, not ours. Affiliate programs may set their own cookies once you land on the provider’s site. We have no control over, and take no responsibility for, third-party practices. Your rights Because we don’t collect personal data, there’s nothing for us to export or delete. If that ever changes, we’ll update this page first. Questions? Contact us .

name: Affiliate Disclosure
description: How Movelli makes money: we use affiliate links and may earn a commission, at no extra cost to you. It never changes our recommendations.
articleBody:
Affiliate Disclosure

Movelli is free to read and carries no display advertising. We fund the site through affiliate partnerships . This page explains exactly what that means. What an affiliate link is Some outbound links to providers (such as eSIM apps, VPNs and banks) are affiliate links. If you sign up or buy through one, the provider may pay us a commission. You pay exactly the same price — often less, when we can pass on a deal. How it affects what we recommend It doesn’t. We recommend products on merit. We’re happy to feature providers that don’t pay us a cent, and we’ll tell you when a free option beats a paid one. If a recommendation ever reads like an ad, we’ve failed — please tell us . How you can spot them Affiliate links are marked up with rel="sponsored" and typically open in a new tab. We don’t hide them, and you’re never required to use them — going directly to a provider works just as well. A note for the FTC In line with US Federal Trade Commission guidance, we disclose that Movelli has material affiliate relationships with some of the providers mentioned across this site.
